<reason>CON built a tight structural case that the motion's hinge—individual opt-in—does no real work once PRO's own concessions are mapped: forbidden monitoring is settled by limits (PRO agreed "consent was never a solvent"), necessary monitoring is collected regardless (PRO's A1 allowed a scoped file record from a declining trainee), so consent governs only the middle tier of unjustifiable monitoring, which the motion makes purchasable from the least-leveraged worker. PRO's best counters were real: CON's necessity standard does admit some video without individual consent (login face check, trader task camera), and "necessity" is elastic. But CON plausibly distinguished a brief on-worker face check from a living-room feed and stressed that the full kitchen camera is illegal under CON's rule while legal for the signer under the motion. PRO's enforcement answer on the loyalty test (grievance tools, assignment patterns) was weak, and PRO's own concession that "soft favoritism exists wherever a right exists" hurt. PRO never fully escaped the opening dilemma: if consent is truly costless, why would anyone sign, and if not costless, it launders. CON's two clipped turns are an execution cost and keep the margin modest, but the essential content survived. Both sides argued with grounded, plausible reasoning and no fake sourcing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–B2.4: CON seized PRO's line "If fraud detection needs a log, collect the log," showed that under the motion's text keystroke monitoring is gated by opt-in, and then mapped PRO's concessions to argue consent only governs monitoring PRO's own necessity test says has "failed"—forcing PRO into the awkward file-log-isn't-keystroke distinction for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
